original_question: Determine what biological predictions are made by evaluating knowledge-based movement models using the net-growth measure based on reaction terms, including whether there are optimal cognition-related parameter ranges and how those predictions compare with a null model that lacks cognition-based movement.
target_in_paper: Open Problem 41 in Section 4.2.1 ("Measures with population dynamics"), posed immediately after the net-growth fitness definition (4.5) for knowledge-based movement models with reaction terms. ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the three main ingredients of the paper’s official formulation: it uses the net-growth fitness measure tied to reaction terms, asks whether cognition-related parameters have optimal ranges, and asks for comparison with a null-hypothesis model without cognition-based movement mechanisms. ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))
missing_details: The paper frames this as an open problem, not as an established result: it asks what consequences and predictions are produced by the measure, rather than asserting that those predictions are already known. ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

The scope is restricted to knowledge-based movement formulations with explicit population dynamics, specifically the models the paper says appear at the end of Section 2.2 and throughout Section 2.3. ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

A stand-alone version should define the variables and functional explicitly: u(x,t) is population density on a spatial domain Ω over a prescribed time interval (t', t_max), and the net-growth fitness measure is Net Growth = ∫_{t'}^{t_max}∫_Ω f(x,t,u) dx dt, where f is the explicit growth/death reaction term. ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

The reaction-term form (4.5) comes from the prior definition Net Growth = ∫_{t'}^{t_max}∫_Ω ∂_t u(x,t) dx dt together with the Section 4.1 conservation discussion, under which the movement terms vanish after spatial integration. ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

The paper treats this as a relative, not absolute, fitness notion: higher net growth means the corresponding model formulation is judged fitter. ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

The example cognition parameters named in the paper are perceptual radius and advection rate toward or away from environmental covariates; these should appear explicitly in the refined question. ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

The nearby context says numerical exploration is likely the main route, while analytic parameter dependence may be feasible when the time interval is chosen so that u(x,t) is close to a temporally constant steady state u*(x). ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

A paper-faithful formulation should record the caveat that, because measure (4.5) depends only on the explicit population dynamics, the influence of different cognitive mechanisms may be lost when a zero-flux boundary condition is used. ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

Items such as ambient ring/field, homogeneity, degree restrictions, nilpotency, and quantifiers like "for all sufficiently large m" are not applicable here; the relevant formal data are instead the PDE variables u, x, t, the domain Ω, the reaction term f, the time interval, and the boundary-condition assumptions. ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))
refined_question: For a knowledge-based animal movement PDE with explicit population dynamics, let u(x,t) denote population density on a spatial domain Ω over a prescribed time interval (t', t_max), and define relative fitness by Net Growth(u) = ∫_{t'}^{t_max}∫_Ω f(x,t,u) dx dt, where f(x,t,u) is the explicit growth/death reaction term obtained after spatial integration removes the movement terms. What biological consequences and predictions does this fitness measure produce for such models? In particular, do cognition-dependent parameters—especially perceptual radius and advection rate toward or away from environmental covariates—admit optimal ranges that increase relative fitness in this sense, and how does that fitness comparison differ from the corresponding null-hypothesis model with no cognitive-based movement mechanism? ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, under the conservation setup discussed in Section 4.1, one may pose the same question using Net Growth = ∫_{t'}^{t_max}∫_Ω ∂_t u(x,t) dx dt, since the paper explicitly derives the reaction-term form (4.5) from this definition when the movement terms vanish after integration. ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))
justification: The nearest official target is Open Problem 41, not the neighboring eigenvalue-based Open Problem 42 or the resource-based Open Problem 43. Your draft is close because it preserves the net-growth/reaction-term fitness lens, the search for optimal cognition parameters, and the comparison with a no-cognition baseline. To make it fully stand-alone and paper-faithful, however, it needed the exact functional (4.5), the scope restriction to models with population dynamics, the interpretation of fitness as relative rather than absolute, and the Section 4.1/4.2.1 caveat that zero-flux settings can suppress how much the metric reflects cognitive movement itself. The introduction and abstract also confirm that the paper uses such measures of success to compare predictions and outcomes of knowledge-based movement models. ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))
